utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I should start by asking the Registrar to announce the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-87/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now, I wish you welcome. Welcome to the parties, welcome to Mr. Djordjevic, welcome to everyone in and especially around the courtroom. We are here today to have the second status conference, because it was 120 days since we were here last. And as you know, according to the Rules, we are required to check up on how you're doing, Mr. Djordjevic, and how the case is progressing, by having a status conference every four months. We have, on the agenda today, just a few points to raise. The -- Mr. Djordjevic, can you hear me in a language ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There is no translation in Serbian for the accused Djordjevic. Something is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shall ask the court officer and the interpreters to make sure that the accused can follow us in a language that he understands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do I understand that you are now able to follow us, Mr. Djordjevic? Thank you very much. I should then, for your benefit, just repeat what I just said; namely, that according to our rules, to the Rules of the Tribunal, we are required to meet every four months for the Chamber to check up on how you are doing and how the proceedings against you are progressing, and for you also to address any concerns directly to the Pre-Trial Judge, if you have any concerns to raise. This is why we have these status conferences. We have for today just a few points on the agenda. Most of them deal with disclosure, and I think I would like to take those issues right away, to embark on these issues right away. The issue of pending motions has been resolved, in the sense that there were a couple of motions from other co-accused to access into your file, and equally you had requested access to the material in some other files. All of these decisions have now been -- all of these motions have now been dealt with, and I think that there are no further issues in relation to the issue of access to material. My staff has just reminded me that I still need to ask for the appearance of the parties, and I apologise for that. So I would like the Prosecution to present itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Chester Stamp, and with me is Patricia Neema, and our case manager here today is Mr. Iain Reid. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: For the Defence, the lead counsel, Dragoljub Djordjevic, and then the co-counsel, Mr. Veljko Djurdjic, and legal assistant Ms. Marie O'Leary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. As I said, we have no more issues in relation to access to material. Then, Mr. Djordjevic, your counsel also filed two preliminary motions, one on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and one on the form of the indictment. The first of these preliminary motions has been dealt with, and you may already be aware of the result. We decided to deny that motion or to dismiss it. As for the other motion relating to the defects in the form of the indictment, the problem that is coming up in relation to this motion is that the trial against you was originally, as you know, a part of a trial against a number of other co-accused, Mr. Milutinovic and others. If the fairness of the trial has to be respected, I believe that we shall have to proceed in the trial against you on the same conditions as the trial that is currently pending against Mr. Milutinovic. This may imply that we should not amend or require the Prosecution to seek amendment of your indictment in any way, because we will have to then proceed with a trial against you on exactly the same terms as the terms applied in the trial against Mr. Milutinovic and others. This is why, although there may be reasons to actually seek amendments of the indictment and improvement of some of the issues of the form of the indictment, although I may have good reasons to do so, I still may have to stay away from that possibility in order to ensure that the trial against you is conducted on terms that are not different in any way from the terms of the Milutinovic trial. But let us see how this issue appears once the judgement has been rendered in the Milutinovic trial. Only when the Trial Chamber has completed its proceedings and rendered its judgement will we be able to assess whether there is room for altering the indictment against you, and I have therefore suggested that the Trial Chamber -- or the Pre-Trial Judge, that is, myself, that I will seek to resolve this issue no later than three weeks after the judgement in the Milutinovic case. So as soon as that judgement has been rendered, we will immediately have a look again at your indictment, and if there is room for any amendments, we will have them made very quickly. As far as disclosure is concerned -- Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering, Your Honour, if the agenda or the way in which you intend to conduct these proceedings would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I may interpose something here, since you're moving on to something else, or if I should await all of your comments before seeking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's in respect to the comments you made about the timing of a decision on the motion of the Defence on the form of the indictment. At the status -- at the Rule 65 ter decision discussions yesterday, at that meeting I had indicated that there was some uncertainty about when we could expect a judgement in the Milutinovic case, and I have reflected upon what I said and have had discussions with other persons involved in that case, and it is probably unlikely that we could expect a decision in that case in a time frame that would enable the Court -- or this Trial Chamber to abide by the schedule I see at items 8 and 9 of the work plan. It might well be that a judgement in the Milutinovic case might not be granted -- not might well be; it is probable that it will not be rendered before those dates. So I wish to bring that to the Court's attention that perhaps that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I think we shall revert to that issue when we get to points 8 and 9 on my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. The other comment I wanted to make, to tell the Court, that the Prosecution in this case had intended to apply to amend the indictment. We were hoping to have the judgement or the decision on the form of the indictment first, before we made an application -- but we do intend at some point in time to make an application, and this would be base of the experience that we have had in the Milutinovic case. And on the basis of that experience, we believe that perhaps an amendment to the indictment in some areas, not necessarily in the issue as to mode of liability, but as far as some of the incidents that are named are concerned, may well be more illustrated -- may advance the ability of the Trial Chamber to do justice in the case. So I just give notice that that is something the Prosecution is considering, and to some extent that might well depend on the timing of a decision on the form of the indictment. Thank you very much for allowing me to interpose here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. My suggestion would be that we seek -- you may sit -- that we seek to raise this issue in a 65 ter meeting quite soon, where we can sit down with the Defence and evaluate or assess the areas in which it might be possible to call for an amendment of the indictment at this early time, but I will get back to you both, both the Prosecution and the Defence, on this issue when we have had a chance to look at it again. Mr. Djordjevic, do you have anything to add to what Mr. Stamp has made known to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Not for now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as disclosure is concerned, I understand that the supporting material has, even a long time ago, been handed over to the Defence in a hard copy and in a language that the accused understands, so that's not an issue any longer. But as far as the issue of hard copies was concerned, an exchange of letters has been held between the parties in which your Defence counsel, Mr. Djordjevic, has asked that you be provided with a hard copy of all the supporting material and the statements that will follow according to Rule 66(A)(ii). We were also informed that you had been given a small computer in the Detention Unit, but that there was a problem because you were, at present, not able to fully use that computer. We therefore inquired with the Detention Unit whether it was possible to provide some training for you, and I have been informed by the UNDU that there is a computer support clerk available in the prison and that the person is able to teach you the basic steps to use the computer and how to open the CDs and the DVDs that you get from the Prosecution. I also understand that there was a course offered to the detainees and that each of the detainees who wished to avail themselves to this course were required to sign up for the course. I don't know if you have done so, but if you have not, I strongly invite you to sign up for the course and to make yourself available to the teaching that is offered in the UNDU so that you can use the computer and open the CDs that are provided to you. It's much, much easier to handle things by way of a computer than it is to have a lot of paper stored in your room at the Detention Unit, and I'm sure that you will, with some practice, be able to appreciate the advantages of using a computer. So I warmly and strongly encourage you and invite you to make use of this option. In relation to the issue of disclosure of witness statements from witnesses that are going to be called at trial, of course, this does in some respects depend on which witnesses the Prosecution, in the end, decides to call - not until then, of course, will it be possible to say exactly which statements they should give to you - but as I did yesterday in the 65 ter meeting, I will repeat again here in open court that I invite and encourage the Prosecution to make available to Mr. Djordjevic and the Defence statements of witnesses whom you already at this time will know for sure that you will call at trial, so that the Defence can start working on these statements as soon as possible. I also understand that there was an issue of the Defence getting a number of DVDs from the Prosecution, and we witnessed yesterday that an exchange was made. And I don't know if, in the meantime, you, Mr. Djordjevic, if you have had the time to check whether these new DVDs that you got can be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we checked all DVDs, and it's all right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm relieved to hear this and thank the Prosecution for providing the new materials. And should it ever happen again, that the DVDs cannot be opened, then please do not hesitate to contact Mr. Stamp or Mr. Hannis right away, or the case manager, so that you can have the problem resolved. The next issue is the issue of disclosure of exculpatory material, and this, as you may know, Mr. Djordjevic, is an obligation that is incumbent on the Prosecution. It's an ongoing obligation, so as soon as the Prosecution discovers that it has material that might be exculpatory for you, it has the obligation to immediately provide this information to you. So no time limit can or should be set for this. This is an obligation that applies to the Prosecution at all times. But there is one thing that will facilitate this process, and that is the extent in which the Defence is able to identify, search -- or key words by which searches can be made for exculpatory material. This is not something that can be done at this moment, probably, because it takes time for the Defence to get accustomed to the case and to get into the case, and not until the Defence counsel has had a chance to really go through all the material will you be able to identify key words that will then enable the Prosecution to search for further exculpatory material. But this is something that really requires a close cooperation between the parties. You may already at this point have been made aware of certain key points that you want the Prosecution to apply in its search for exculpatory material, and so I would imagine that you, every now and then, contact the Prosecution and ask for searches to be made on these issues, rather than waiting to the end and coming up with all of your key words, then you might want to discuss this with the Prosecution and have them make searches every now and then as soon as you have discovered new key words that you wish to you to apply. I guess this is the sensible way of getting around the searches. Each of the parties will, at trial, present expert witnesses, and each of the witnesses will present expert reports, and I imagine that the Prosecution will be able to, fairly soon, to identify the experts that they wish to bring at trial. And I would ask them to identify their expert witnesses and to submit the reports of these expert witnesses before 15th of March of this year, and I hope that the Prosecution is ready and willing to do so. Can you confirm that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are in a position to abide by that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That sounds good. And then as we get closer to trial, we will expect to see lists of witnesses and motions filed under Rule 92 bis and 92 ter and 92 quater, but I think we should not set any time limit for this at this moment. It is simply too early and the trial is too far away for us to handle this with any degree of precision. So let us wait until we get closer to the beginning of the trial, and we can then set deadlines for submission of these motions. The same goes for the attempts to identify facts adjudicated in previous trials. Of course, the first trial -- the first judgement that we will look into is the Milutinovic judgement, and not until that has been rendered will we be able to see a motion in regard to taking judicial notice of facts that have been adjudicated in that judgement. Finally, the issue of alibi, according to Rule 67 of the Rules, if the Defence intends to present the defence of alibi on behalf of Mr. Djordjevic, the Defence will be requested to do so no later than two weeks before the Prosecution's pre-trial brief so that we can give the Prosecution a bit of time to respond to such a claim for alibi. And this is where we come to the points 8 and 9 on the work plan. We had anticipated, in the Chamber, that the trial could possibly start sometime in the fall of this year; October, November, December. And if that were so, we would then ask the parties to present their pre-trial briefs a couple of months ahead of that, so that we would expect the Prosecution to submit its pre-trial brief sometime in July and the Defence, respectively, to file its pre-trial brief sometime in August. Now, Mr. Stamp, you just suggested that we may be speaking of something that we have not understood fully, so will you please enlighten us as to what the prospects are for the rendering of the judgement in Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From this side, it is really a matter of estimation. I think the Chamber itself could indicate when it is likely that a judgement could be rendered. What I can say is that in discussion with counsel in the Milutinovic case, we were seeking a period of two to three months from the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when do you have the end of the hearings in Milutinovic? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I was saying we were having discussions, and in that discussions we were seeking of the Chamber a time frame of two to three months from the end of the reception of evidence to the closing brief of the parties. So if the evidence -- if the trial, in terms of the evidence, ends in March or April, we were speaking about June, and I'm sure the Chamber would need some time, in a case that has gone on for two years at a very hectic pace, to deliver its judgement. So the judgement, it is my estimation, and I can only estimate, is unlikely to be rendered in the first half of this year. It is probably going to be rendered after the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree, and this was also the premise on which our estimation was based. When I said that the earliest possible time the trial against Mr. Djordjevic could start would be sometime in the fall, that corresponds and coincides, actually, with your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We were thinking that perhaps it might be -- it might present us some difficulty to go ahead with a pre-trial brief without having had the benefit of the decision on the form of the indictment. We were of the view that the indictment itself should be settled before we reach that stage, not only in terms of any alteration that might have to be made, having regard to the decision itself, but also how the Court would receive and deal with any application -- or [indiscernible] that you expect to make to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I was under the impression, when we had the meeting yesterday, that you would prefer the Chamber to pursue the line that we have taken so far, that is to say to simply wait, but I now hear you saying that you would actually wish to see a decision on the form of the indictment earlier than that. If I had not misunderstood, then, this is a slightly new version of the Prosecution's view --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I fully respect that, and I think upon your call, we will then revisit our decision to postpone the decision on the form of the indictment and maybe actually hand down a decision pretty soon, because, you see, if the indictment won't change much anyway, then there is no reason to wait. Then we might as well say, well, the indictment stands as it stands, because Mr. Djordjevic should be tried on the same conditions as Mr. Milutinovic and the other co-accused in that case, so we'll just simply confirm the indictment as it is now, and then only perhaps open for a review if that is called for by the -- upon delivery of the judgement in Milutinovic. And if you think this is a wise approach, and I have much sympathy for that, then I think this is what we'll do. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: By your permission, Your Honour, I will continue in B/C/S, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Your Honour, personally I believe that apart from the trial -- to the right of a fair trial, each accused has the right to stand trial within a reasonable period of time. Since this accused was a part of the same indictment with the other accused in the Milutinovic case, and concerning the right he has you mentioned, to be tried under the same conditions as the other accused were, and especially having in mind the fact that the Prosecutor, up to the tiniest detail when forwarding all of the documents supporting the indictment against Milutinovic et al, which was subsequently broadened to include our accused, Mr. Djordjevic, the situation is, in my opinion, that the Prosecution, as of that moment and in relation to the so-called "Kosovo case," which is Milutinovic et al, has definitive and detailed knowledge concerning Mr. Djordjevic himself. Therefore, it is my position that the Prosecution can do that straight away. This Defence has no such information, and by being forced to wait, we will be put in a position not to be able to execute our tasks with due diligence, unless the Prosecutor is going to submit all of the material within a reasonable time. That is why I believe, first of all respecting the right to have a trial held within a reasonable time and the right to a fair trial, the Prosecution could have already amended the indictment pertaining to Mr. Djordjevic. There will be nothing new after the Milutinovic judgement, I believe, at least not on the Prosecution side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Whether or not the judgement in Milutinovic will allow for amendments of the indictment against Mr. Djordjevic still remains to be seen, but I hear both parties being in agreement of the Chamber handing down a decision on the form of the indictment upon your motion, Mr. Djordjevic, and if this is correctly understood, the Chamber will proceed to issue its decision to respond to your motion. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would agree that that is the position. But to clarify, I just point out that having regard to the dates here, it is the position of the Prosecution -- the recommendation of the Prosecution that it is best if the indictment is settled before those dates, and that is all I wish to point out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is obvious, so we'll proceeding accordingly. And we will then, if needed, be able to review the dates that we have suggested for submission of the pre-trial briefs, once we have issued the decision, but I thank you both for your willingness to go along this line and for your submissions in this respect. I think this pretty much brings us to the end of what I had on my agenda, except for one thing, and that is to address the issue of your health, Mr. Djordjevic. I wish to know if you are in good health and shape and if you have any concerns that you wish to raise with me at this moment concerning your conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to say about the Detention Unit. My conditions are the same as the others. As for the use of the PC, I am really not capable of learning anything, and I believe that I should be able and should be allowed to work with papers, because that is the only way I can actually peruse all the material and be able to respond to any motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. I'm happy to hear that you are at least in good health. As far as the provision of hard copies is concerned, I think your Defence counsel will provide you with the hard copies of the things that the Prosecution is not required to submit to you in hard copy, according to the Rules. So whatever the Prosecution has to give to you in hard copy, it will give to you in hard copy, and the rest will then be provided by your Defence counsel. Now, in order to make life easier also for your Defence counsel, it would be a big help for your Defence counsel and thereby also for me or for the Chamber if you could learn how to use a computer. It's not that difficult, and I'm sure you will have great fun in learning how to do this. So in your own interests and in the interests of your Defence counsel, and thereby in the interests of the Chamber, I would, again as I said, encourage you to pick it up and to take the training that can be offered and can be arranged for you in the Detention Unit. You probably don't need more than, I don't know, five, ten, maybe to fifteen lessons with a computer teacher in the Detention Unit, and then you will be fully capable of using your computer. If the parties do not have any other issues to raise, and I wish to ask the parties if this is so, the Prosecution, do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Nothing to raise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. D. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, we can conclude this status conference, and we will meet again in about four months' time. And I'll let you know, through my staff, who can suggest new dates for the next meeting. Thank you very much. This meeting is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
